title: Penelope Cruz to Star in and Produce Netflix Drama ‘Patricia’ From ‘On the Fringes’ Director Juan Diego Botto
description: Penélope Cruz, who is emerging as a major contender in this year’s Oscar race with a trio of films, is set to star and produce “Patricia,” a Netfli
body:
Penélope Cruz, who is emerging as a major contender in this year’s Oscar race with a trio of films, is set to star and produce “Patricia,” a Netflix drama written and directed by Juan Diego Botto.

	Set to start filming soon, “Patricia” marks the first narrative feature produced by Moonlyon, the production company Cruz launched in partnership with Imagina.

	The film reteams Cruz with Botto following his feature debut “On the Fringes,” a socially minded drama.  
	

	Cruz stars as Patricia, a woman who escapes a 12-year abusive relationship only to find herself facing another ordeal in the courts, where she fears for the well-being of her children.

	The cast also includes Goya Toledo (“Amores Perros,” “Marsella”), Ramón Barea (“Lullaby,” “Everybody Knows”) and Dylan Radley.

	“After two years of writing and a long research process, which included hours of interviews with women who trusted us with their stories, it is a privilege for me to tell this story with this cast and this creative team,” Botto said.

	Cruz said she had also been involved in developing “Patricia” alongside Botto for over two years.  

	”I feel enormous excitement,” Cruz said. “It has been a beautiful and intense journey alongside my dear Juan Diego Botto. Juan has written a wonderful script, and it is an honor to tell this story with him.”

	“It is a very necessary story, and an immense privilege to play this character. Patricia represents so many other women who, like her, suffer this kind of violence every day,” she continued. 
	

	The actor also praised Netflix’s Spanish team. “This is my first film with them, and we couldn’t be happier with the care and attention they have shown us,” she said.

	Diego Ávalos, Netflix’s VP of content for Spain, Portugal, Turkey and the Middle East, highlighted the film’s international resonance.

	“Some stories matter to us for what they tell and how they are told, and Patricia is one of those rare and unforgettable stories: brave and courageous, brought to life by an extraordinary team,” Ávalos said. “I’m truly honored to join Juan Diego Botto and Penélope Cruz in their first film for Netflix in Spain, and for a story born at home to move audiences here and around the world.”

	Cruz is a contender in the 2027 awards race with three films, including Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” directed by Javier Ambrossi et Javier Calvo, as well as Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” and Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite.”

title: Backed by Honorary Oscar Winner Christine Vachon, Ray Panthaki’s Directorial Debut ‘In Starland’ Marks a ‘Coming-of-Middle-Age Story’
description:
British actor Ray Panthaki – known for “Boiling Point” and “Marcella” – goes personal in directorial debut “In Starland.” Very personal.

	His firs
body:
British actor Ray Panthaki – known for “Boiling Point” and “Marcella” – goes personal in directorial debut “In Starland.” Very personal.

	His first feature is produced by his London-based Le Bateau Lavoir, Archface Films and Killer Films, headed by Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, who have just been presented wih Honorary Oscars. Variety announced Killer Films boarding “In Starland” in October. “In Starland” world-premieres at Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival.
	

	“I was a young carer and often felt I hadn’t come of age when society tells you that you’re supposed to. I had responsibilities that most people my age didn’t,” Panthaki tells Variety. “That changed when my acting career took off in my early twenties, but I’d carried this thought around: what if someone got to their forties and had never really lived? I found that quite heartbreaking, but also full of possibility.”

	He adds: “It might never be too late to become the person you were supposed to be.”

	Ernie (Clarence Maclin) is about to discover this when his quiet, unremarkable life in a small American town is turned upside down by a group of young influencers who force him out of his shell. Panthaki describes his film as a “coming-of-middle-age story.”

	“I don’t believe that becoming yourself is something reserved for the young. Sometimes it takes half a lifetime to understand what’s been holding you back, and perhaps another half to do something about it.”

	His characters keep on fighting: for companionship – like Ernie – or for internet fame and glory like some of his new friends. What unites them is loneliness.
	

	“It’s something I’ve experienced myself, and I’ve seen people very close to me go through it. Particularly with older people, there’s something about someone having lived this entire life and then finding themselves alone that I find incredibly moving. It wasn’t really a question of whether I’d explore it, but when,” notes Panthaki. He calls loneliness “one of the great contradictions of our time.”

	“We’ve never been more connected, and yet we seem to be feeling more disconnected than ever.”

	“I suppose that’s where the film becomes quite spiritual for me. Beneath all the noise, the technology and performance, we’re all just human beings looking for love, acceptance and a sense of belonging. There’s a big difference between being seen and being known. Maybe that’s what the film is really about.”

	Panthaki has a “huge amount of hope” in the new generation, but also admits they’ve inherited a world where everything is “increasingly measured in numbers.”

	“The irony is that at one point I tried to play that game myself. We’d spent years trying to finance the film, and I thought: Right. If the industry wants numbers, I’ll give them numbers. I’ll cast ten influencers with a combined following of 250 million people. Except I wasn’t particularly comfortable with it,” he recalls.

	He changed his mind, ultimately choosing people who were simply right for the part.

	“No follower counts, no industry heat, no looking at what people had done before,” he says.

	“As an actor, I know what it feels like to be judged on things that have nothing to do with your ability to do the job. I know what it’s like to lose a job when everyone wants you, but the studio wants a bigger name. There was something quite satisfying to finally be in a position to correct some of the things I’d experienced myself.”

	“On the first day of rehearsals, I told the cast that we were going to make this film for every single ‘no’ we’d ever had as artists.”

	For the role of Ernie, Panthaki was looking for someone “who could communicate an entire lifetime without saying very much.”

	“Clarence has this extraordinary quality where you can just stay on his face and feel the weight of everything that’s happened to him. There’s a tremendous vulnerability there, but also something unpredictable and even dangerous,” he says.
	

	“He wasn’t the Ernie I’d imagined when we wrote the script. But there was something in his screen test that I couldn’t ignore – a truth that would be very difficult to manufacture.”

	It wasn’t easy to get “In Starland” off the ground. 

	“I got to make the film I wanted to make, with the people I wanted to make it with, without having to compromise my beliefs. It’s the hardest thing I’ve ever done, but it feels quite fitting to have spent seven years making a film about a man who’s trying to find his own way in the world.”

	He doesn’t like to call it an indie, however.

	“There are films that are considered independent that still have a whole infrastructure of public funding and institutional support behind them. We didn’t have any of that. I’ve embraced the term ‘non-dependent’, which Ted Hope has written about,” he says.

	“So many things that happened throughout this process that I couldn’t have planned or explained. They only strengthened my belief that this was a story I was meant to tell, and that there was a reason it needed to be told now.”

	Panthaki also ignored the naysayers also when completing the soundtrack. Obsessed with ’80s hits, he made sure his characters loved them too.

	“Nothing like disguising your own taste in music as character development! Nostalgia is such a powerful thing. Music can take you back 40 years in a second, and I wanted the audience to feel that. Particularly through Ernie, who’s carrying around a whole lifetime of memories and experiences,” he says. He wrote all the songs into the script.

	“I knew exactly what I wanted and where I wanted it, but getting them was a different story. ‘Everybody Wants to Rule the World’ is one of the greatest songs ever written. It captured so much of what the film was exploring. Power, control, celebrity, and this very human desire to feel important. I couldn’t imagine opening the film any other way.”

	He wrote to some of the musicians personally.

	“We had absolutely no business trying to get [these songs] on our budget, but I’ve always believed in going directly to artists. You’d be surprised how often people want to help when they understand your ‘why’,” he recalls.

	“I’ve spent seven years being told we couldn’t do things. We couldn’t shoot in America on that budget; we couldn’t make it in 20 days; we couldn’t get those actors; we couldn’t afford that music. And we just kept finding ways.”
	

	“There’s very little in this film that we haven’t had to fight for in some way.”

title: YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content
description: YouTube has turned down a request from the British government to remove a video in which Russell Brand claims he is innocent after being sentenced
body:
YouTube has turned down a request from the British government to remove a video in which Russell Brand claims he is innocent after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault, according to the BBC.

	Google, which owns YouTube, said the video did not violate its rules and revealed it was reviewing the content.

	“We are aware of the new content and our teams are investigating,” Google told the BBC in a statement. “We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then,” the company added.  
	

	The controversy follows a YouTube video posted Sunday by Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, in which she addressed the comedian’s conviction before reading a message from him during their “Sunday Service with the Brands” series.

	“As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,” Brand said in the message.

	Gallacher also told viewers that her husband was “okay” and “praying” in prison. The couple, who married in 2017, share three children.

	The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that YouTube remove the video, arguing that it was offensive to Brand’s victims and had reached a substantial audience.

	British officials have criticized Google’s decision, with housing minister Matthew Pennycook describing the video as “abhorrent” and saying the government remained in “close dialogue” with the company, according to the BBC. 
	

	Meanwhile, Meta has disabled Brand’s Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp accounts under its policies prohibiting accounts owned or operated by convicted sex offenders. His YouTube channel and X account remain active.

	British prison authorities are also investigating whether Brand breached prison rules by issuing the statement. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he expected action to be taken if Brand was found to have violated regulations.

schema.headline: YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content

title: Hearst Canvas Launches Frontier Collective Brand as U.K. Arm Builds Digital-Native Content Slate for YouTube
description: Hearst Canvas, the creator-led media arm of U.K.-based Hearst Networks, has launched its latest digital native brand with Frontier Collective, an e
body:
Hearst Canvas, the creator-led media arm of U.K.-based Hearst Networks, has launched its latest digital native brand with Frontier Collective, an effort to harness the YouTube and social media followings of top outdoor adventure content creators.

	The effort has quietly bowed over the past few weeks starting with a roundtable-style talk show, “Expedition HQ,” featuring four prominent U.K. explorers at the core of Frontier Collective: Aldo Kane, Alex Bescoby, Levison Wood and Lucy Shepherd. The foursome come together swap stories about explorations and derring-do in their efforts to explore the natural world and far-flung exotic locales. “Expedition HQ” bowed Nov. 1 on the Frontier Collective YouTube channel, with new episodes released weekly. Clips are spread widely around Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat.
	

	Hearst Canvas hopes to tap into the heat of the adventure content community on YouTube. The Hearst Canvas division is set up to find top-tier creators who can contribute to strong verticals as Hearst Networks develops new content and formats designed to roll out on YouTube. Dean Possenniskie, managing director, Hearst Networks, Europe, Middle East and Africa and managing director Hearst Networks U.K., is overseeing the Canvas venture that was launched in October 2025. 

	“We’ve now built a dedicated creative team that is going to originate formats in a different style that are designed to work as creator-led content on YouTube,” Possenniskie told Variety. “A format like Frontier Collective is unique in the fact it brings together four very strong talents in the space. It’s not an audience that we traditionally reach here in the U.K. through pay TV or DTC or broadcast channels. It’s a global audience, and it’s a much broader audience for us to reach now as well. So that’s a really exciting opportunity.”
	

	Hearst Canvas is headed by Danny Baggot as creative director and Sam Pearson as executive producer. The pair unveiled the venture’s first commission on Oct. 29, the unscripted business revitalization series “Pitch, Please.” 

	“Frontier Collective offers a compelling opportunity to build something unique in the adventure space — a network of remarkable individuals whose passion drives them to explore the far reaches of our globe and share what they’ve experienced with the world,” Pearson said. “And with ‘Expedition HQ,’ we’re launching a returning format that delivers on this promise through fascinating and insightful conversations.”

	The roundtable series is produced by Grammar Productions, co-founded by Bescoby. It’s produced shows for BBC, Channel 4, Apple TV, Amazon Prime, Discovery, Sky HISTORY and Canal+, in addition to custom work for brands. 

	As a veteran of the adventure genre, Bescoby said he sees demand for Frontier Collective as a concept.

	“Some of the best adventure storytellers I know have spent years asking for a proper home for their work,” Bescoby said. “Traditional television has stepped back from the genre, even as audiences are clamoring for more. It’s hugely exciting that Hearst Canvas is building that home with Frontier Collective, and it’s amazing to be a part of it.”

	Kane invoked the importance of the YouTube channel as serving as a hub for adventure content fan communities. “This new YouTube channel allows us to bring directly to our community the real story that goes on behind the scenes on these adventures,” he said.

	Wood added that every major adventure yields its own unique experiences, and inevitably, there is more color than can be included in the final program. “So much never makes it into the finished documentaries. I’m looking forward to sharing more of those experiences and unseen footage on my own channels as part of Frontier Collective,” Wood said.

	Shepherd added her enthusiasm for the push to build a hub for top digital-native explorers and adventurers. 

	“I’m only sorry this didn’t begin sooner. There’s something very special about sitting around a table with people whose adventures inspired me to set out on my own,” Shepherd said. “Life is an expedition, and I hope our stories inspire others to find a little adventure in their lives, wherever they are.”
	

	(Pictured: “Expedition HQ” hosts Alex Bescoby, Lucy Shepherd, Levison Wood and Aldo Kane)

schema.headline: Hearst Canvas Launches Frontier Collective Brand as U.K. Arm Builds Digital-Native Content Slate for YouTube

title: Jeon Do-yeon on Oscar Contender ‘Possible Love,’ Korean Cinema’s Commercial Pull and Her ‘Greater Thirst’ for Stories
description: Korean actors are far better known around the world today than when Jeon Do-yeon won best actress at Cannes for Lee Chang-dong’s “Secret Sunshine”
body:
Korean actors are far better known around the world today than when Jeon Do-yeon won best actress at Cannes for Lee Chang-dong’s “Secret Sunshine” in 2007, becoming the first Korean actress to do so. She has asked herself what that should change about the work she picks, and her answer is to stay on the path she has always been on.

	“Possible Love,” also from Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong, is a Venice competition title that also screened at the Busan and Toronto. It is South Korea’s submission for the Oscars’ international feature category. Jeon plays Mi-ok, a mask-factory worker whose husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), has been laid off. Produced by Pinehouse Film, Anonymous Content, Nowfilm and Netflix, the film opened in theaters Oct. 23 and has been streaming on the platform since Nov. 6.
	

	Jeon says the projects she is drawn to are “a little bit different from what is globally loved and known these days, so to speak.” She asked herself whether she could say yes immediately to projects with wider global appeal, and concluded “I wouldn’t say yes to that.” “I think I’m probably going to continue to go down the path that I have always been going down, and go in my own direction,” she says.

	Her frustration sits closer to home. She says she doesn’t know about the American market, but within Korea “the focus is not so much about the story or the project itself, but a lot of it is focused on commercial appeal.” In her view, “there is less time being spent on really struggling with what the story holds, what the character is all about,” and she says she feels sorry to see that happen.
	

	She is not hunting for a particular role, Jeon says, but “I do feel that I have a greater thirst for the stories themselves.” “‘Possible Love’ is so significant for me at this juncture in my career, and also something that I’m just so grateful to be a part of,” she says.

	She found her way into Mi-ok through shared worry. “I thought that the anxiety she harbors in her heart was something that I could relate to, because I also have that as well,” Jeon says. Mi-ok, she says, “has a ticking time bomb in her heart, almost, because she’s always anxious about when Ho-seok is going to explode,” and she and Mi-ok share “a sense of wanting life to be uneventful.”

	Her read on Mi-ok’s pull toward Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), the wealthy husband of a documentary filmmaker, changed once cameras rolled. On the page, Jeon says, it looked like desire for a man she saw as “someone like Steve Jobs who could probably solve all of your problems.” In performance, “I came to think that it’s more about curiosity,” she says, “curiosity about a life that’s different.”

	Mi-ok’s resilience felt familiar too. Someone once told Jeon that, in the face of hardship, she is not the type to lie down and cry. Mi-ok, she says, is “the type of person who will get up and try her best not to let go of hope.”

	Working with Lee again was easier than the first time. On “Secret Sunshine,” Jeon says, “the relationship or the mood on set, it was very intense,” and “I was so filled with self-doubt that it made communication between the director and myself very difficult.” Going in this time, she says, she was “a little bit anxious about how it was going to be, but to my pleasant surprise, I felt so comfortable and so much at ease when I stepped onto the set.”

	Lee, she adds, “was more prepared for working with me,” and the overall mood “was a lot more relaxed than before.”

	Jeon says she is considering a film for her next project, “but nothing has been decided yet.” She says she looks forward to telling greater stories and finding those works.

schema.headline: Jeon Do-yeon on Oscar Contender ‘Possible Love,’ Korean Cinema’s Commercial Pull and Her ‘Greater Thirst’ for Stories

title: ‘Ramayana’ Journey Across Asia Anchors Discovery India Docuseries Marking Shashi Tharoor’s TV Hosting Debut (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Author and Indian lawmaker Shashi Tharoor is making his debut as a TV host, fronting “Itihasa: Ramayana Beyond Borders With Shashi Tharoor,” a four
body:
Author and Indian lawmaker Shashi Tharoor is making his debut as a TV host, fronting “Itihasa: Ramayana Beyond Borders With Shashi Tharoor,” a four-part Discovery docuseries that follows the ancient Indian epic as it spread to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

	The series will premiere Dec. 7 in India on Discovery and Discovery+, with one new episode each week. It will be available in the English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malayalam and Kannada languages. 
	

	A trailer has been unveiled.

	Each episode centers on one of the story’s four principal figures – Rama, Hanuman, Ravana and Sita – and examines how depictions of that character have changed from one culture to the next.

	With India as its point of origin, the show visits Cambodia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia to look at the shared history and cultural contact that allowed the epic to settle in each country. It also considers how regional history, religious belief and art gave rise to distinct versions of the tale, which successive generations in different places adopted and reworked.

	The show arrives with the “Ramayana” already dominating global cinemas. Nitesh Tiwari’s big-screen adaptation “Ramayana: Part 1,” starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Yash as Ravana and Sai Pallavi as Sita, opened Nov. 5 and grossed $147 million worldwide in its first 11 days.

	“The ‘Ramayana’ is a remarkable example of how a story can cross seas and find new life in other civilizations,” Tharoor said.

	Sai Abishek, head of factual entertainment, lifestyle and kids for South Asia at Skydance, said the team worked with scholars and practitioners from several countries, who also appear in the series. On-screen contributors range from historians, religious scholars and Sanskrit specialists to heritage researchers and traditional artists.
	

	Abishek said many viewers know the Ramayana through the tradition nearest to them, “but its journey across Asia reveals a much larger cultural inheritance.”

	The show is the first title under ‘Itihasa,’ a new Discovery franchise built around stories drawn from India’s past and its cultural legacy, approached from a broader perspective.

	Abishek said the network was thrilled to have Tharoor on board, adding: “His understanding of history and literature, and his ability to make complex ideas engaging, will help audiences navigate the many perspectives at the heart of the series.”

	Tharoor added that literature, history and cultural exchange had long been abiding interests of his, “which made this an especially fitting subject for my debut as a television host. I am delighted that this first step has been with Discovery.”

title: ‘Steps’ Review: Brightly Colored, Harmless Reimagining of ‘Cinderella’ Packs Funny Lines but Little That’s Unique
description: As revisionist narratives that seek to rehabilitate a villain’s reputation, “Shrek” and “Wicked” have set the standard for what this type of altern
body:
As revisionist narratives that seek to rehabilitate a villain’s reputation, “Shrek” and “Wicked” have set the standard for what this type of alternative fairytale can look like, whether comic or dramatic. The new Netflix animated feature “Steps” follows in the footsteps of those more accomplished predecessors, showing that Cinderella’s stepsisters may have been more nuanced characters than just evildoers standing in the way of a pristine princess.
	

	Veteran animator John Ripa (a co-director on the Oscar-nominated “Raya and the Last Dragon”) joins creative forces with first-time feature director Alyce Tzue for a reimagining of the timeless yarn that introduces new lore — the harmless results are consistently funny, but convoluted and emotionally shorthanded. Here, the spotlight is not on Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) herself, but rather her stepsibling Lilith (Ali Wong), an angsty goth-girl type with a Hot Topic look.

	Lilith and her younger sister Margot (Stephanie Hsu) arrived at the kingdom of Alouette a decade earlier when their mother, a traveling seamstress, fell for Cinderella’s father. A schism in their relationship with their new stepsister formed early — following an incident where Cinderella, afraid of being ostracized, didn’t stand up for Lilith and Margot. Now, as a teen, Lilith loathes Cinderella’s picture-perfect personality. Through a series of magic-driven ordeals, “Steps” sees them trying to mend their bond. 

	That Lilith and Margot are the only Asian girls in this white society is never addressed in a significant manner. Indeed, a musical number, which gives Seyfried a new chance to sing, implies people in town don’t like Lilith and Margot only because they assume the girls bully Cinderella.
	

	Since Cinderella and Lilith aren’t portrayed as mutual antagonists, but instead as misunderstood counterparts, the film introduces Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), a self-centered girl envious of anyone who gets more attention than her. And Priscilla has a henchman, Roderick (Peter Dinklage), who is the film’s most memorable side character — his unrequited fatherly adoration for her driving his murderous determination to please her every command.

	There’s plenty of invention here, as Cinderella’s entire story as we know it comes to pass before the film’s halfway point, leaving extensive room for “Steps” to take the characters into new territory. It certainly does, but with mixed results.

	Given that this story hinges on Cinderella and Lilith’s wish for sisterhood, it’s odd that the 10 years between their initial rift and the present are brushed over so quickly, as is the family dynamic that allowed the grudge to persist. Was Lilith encouraged to develop a relationship with her stepsister? Does Cinderella have a good relationship with her stepmother — a character who is virtually absent for most of the film? By the same token, how did Lilith and Margot feel about their stepdad? Early on, a brief scene shows the whole family eating dumplings together, but that’s the extent of the parents’ involvement. 

	In an overstuffed plot, the time not spent on developing that familial foundation is filled instead with expected appearances by the Fairy Godmother (a wonderful Bette Midler) and the prince (Daniel Radcliffe), but also a romantic interest for Lilith, multiple chases, and eventually even time travel as a solution to the conflict. 

	With five credited writers, the script for “Steps” feels like a too-many-cooks situation, with emotional cohesion sidestepped for boisterous action. What they do deliver on, however, is humor. Numerous one-liners, often cleverly mocking the tropes of the fairytale, land with the desired irreverence. And that comedy holds together various more disparate elements that ultimately fail to come across as singular. 

	Though the kingdom is intricately conceived in gorgeous pastel colors, the character design, while not aesthetically unpleasant, can best be described as standard — the way most 3DCG humans look in mainstream animated features. When Margot (a character with little to do) turns into an adorable, pudgy frog, her design — with her hair buns becoming the creature’s bugging eyes — provides a rare interesting edge to the film’s mostly generic visual identity. The brightly colored world of “Steps,” as well as its use of pop songs and the contentious banter between Wong and Seyfried, may work well enough to entertain young viewers, but it doesn’t make for a classic.

schema.headline: ‘Steps’ Review: Brightly Colored, Harmless Reimagining of ‘Cinderella’ Packs Funny Lines but Little That’s Unique

title: Airbnb Recreates Iconic ‘Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham’ Mansion for Film’s 25th Anniversary, With Kareena Kapoor Khan and Hrithik Roshan Hosting
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Airbnb is
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Airbnb is bringing one of Bollywood’s most recognizable homes to life in celebration of the 25th anniversary of Karan Johar’s “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham.”

	The company has recreated the Raichand family mansion from the 2001 film for a limited-time immersive experience in Mumbai, inviting fans to explore its grand staircase, family study and Poo’s extravagant closet. The two-hour experience, titled “At Home with the Raichands,” will run from Dec. 1-6, with just 180 guest spots available.
	

	The experience is being presented by Johar alongside Hrithik Roshan and Kareena Kapoor Khan, who played Rohan Raichand and Poo, respectively, in the film. The three stars will not appear in person

	Released in December 2001, “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham,” commonly known as “K3G,” featured an ensemble cast including Amitabh Bachchan, Jaya Bachchan, Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol. The family drama, which follows a wealthy Indian family divided by a son’s marriage against his father’s wishes, became one of the defining Bollywood films of its era, with its elaborate production design, musical numbers and fashion continuing to resonate with younger audiences.



	

	





	

	



	The Airbnb recreation will allow guests to explore the mansion through an immersive audio tour featuring memorable moments from the film. Visitors can also step inside a recreation of Poo’s wardrobe, participate in a character-inspired entry challenge and write a personal note inspired by the movie’s themes of love and family. Each guest will receive a commemorative keepsake.

	“Poo has been a part of my life for 25 years, and I love that she’s still having her moment with a whole new generation,” Kapoor Khan said in a statement. “She had her own sense of style, her own vocabulary and, most importantly, she never really needed anyone’s approval.”
	

	Roshan, meanwhile, described the experience as an opportunity to revisit one of his earliest major film roles.

	“To see the Raichand House recreated by Airbnb and to know that fans will get to walk down the memory lane themselves is the best way to celebrate the film,” he said.

	The activation is part of Airbnb’s “Only on Airbnb” experiences, which have increasingly tapped into entertainment properties and fan culture to create real-world versions of fictional settings.

	Booking requests open Nov. 23 at 12 p.m. IST through Airbnb’s dedicated K3G page. The experience is free, with each booking covering two guests, although visitors must arrange their own travel to Mumbai.

schema.headline: Airbnb Recreates Iconic ‘Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham’ Mansion for Film’s 25th Anniversary, With Kareena Kapoor Khan and Hrithik Roshan Hosting

title: ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix FTX Series Fails to Get a Handle on Crypto Scammer Sam Bankman-Fried
description: The collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2022 — a spectacular implosion that saw the company evaporate and sent founder Sam Bankman-Fried to
body:
The collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2022 — a spectacular implosion that saw the company evaporate and sent founder Sam Bankman-Fried to prison, along with much of his inner circle — felt epic in the moment. But compared to the frenzy around artificial intelligence that was soon to come, even the Shakespearean downfall of a corporation that could once casually spend nine figures on stadium naming rights feels like a footnote in the intertwined history of technology and finance. The crypto boom now occupies an awkward middle space in the recent arc of the tech industry: After the Obama-era idealism of Facebook, Twitter and other companies that promised to connect the world for the better and before the full-on dystopian rhetoric of post-human labor and a “permanent underclass.”
	

	The Netflix limited series “The Altruists,” created by Graham Moore (the Oscar-winning screenwriter of “The Imitation Game”) and produced by the Obamas’ shingle Higher Ground, is aware of this gap. “AI is hotter than crypto’s ever been right now,” one character observes in the finale as FTX’s house of cards starts to fall. (Marquee frontier lab and FTX investee Anthropic even makes a cameo.) “The Altruists” could theoretically use our rapidly fading cultural memory to its advantage, dusting off the Bankman-Fried story to deliver a character study that pushes past tabloid headlines about polycules and party mansions to make sense of what happened and a case for why it mattered.

	Instead, “The Altruists” opts for the most conventional, least persuasive lens through which to explain the significance of FTX as well as what went wrong: the on-and-off romance between Bankman-Fried (Irish actor Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner, also an executive producer), the former head of FTX-affiliated hedge fund Alameda Research. The action toggles back and forth between two timelines: the early days of Sam, Caroline and their companies and their swift demise five years later, forecasted in a standard flash-forward to the FBI storming the office.
	

	The erstwhile couple make a certain sense as the show’s focus. They’re a handy metaphor for the messy, inappropriate relationship between their two companies, which culminated in FTX’s use of billions in customer money to cover for Alameda’s trading losses. And, of course, there are salacious details like Ellison’s X-rated “Harry Potter” fanfiction — the kind of low-hanging fruit a writer would have to be foolish to leave on the vine. Sex still sells, even when the sex in question is between socially awkward math geeks whose idea of foreplay is strategic board games.

	But “The Altruists,” which works from a series of New York magazine articles by Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner as its source material, makes Sam and Caroline strangely simplistic, both as individual personalities and larger cultural forces. It starts with the casting: Boyle is a strong actor with a bright future ahead of him; the onetime face of a brash IRA revolutionary in “Say Nothing” is nonetheless an awkward fit for a noted oddball like Bankman-Fried, and Boyle never disappears into the role. His SBF — the boy billionaire’s popular nickname — is motormouthed and visibly anxious, yet the scripts elide some of his strangest tics, like taking interviews while playing video games or sleeping on the office floor. (The bean bag habit is alluded to in dialogue, yet never shown. An odd choice for a visual medium!) Boyle’s performance comes off more like the Mark Zuckerberg of “The Social Network,” a disaffected yet basically relatable nerd who craves validation, than the Mark Zuckerberg of “The Social Reckoning,” a space alien whose inability to grasp human nature has warped the world in his image.

	Garner, for her part, dials up Ellison’s tics into a near-caricature of a four-eyed poindexter. Pre-arrest footage of Ellison, who would go on to cooperate extensively with SBF’s prosecutors, shows the same nervous laughter that Garner accurately mimics, but a much more calm and even speaking voice. Amping up an accent and donning a wig are old hat for the star of “Inventing Anna,” another frustrating Netflix project that captured its subject’s eccentricity without delving into their deeper psychology. Were “The Altruists” more of a straight-up satire in tone, Garner’s caricature might work in context. Instead, isolated moments of humor — upon finding out about the fraud, one FTX employee is mad because he’s been urging them to break the law for years and feels excluded — are left to float in an otherwise sincere story of misguided puppy love. (In a striking detail seemingly invented for the show, Caroline is the first woman Sam ever sleeps with.) Perhaps Moore and co-showrunner Jacqueline Hoyt were worried about crossing over into gleeful cruelty. But if perpetrators of a multibillion dollar fraud don’t deserve some mockery, who does?
	

	Sam and Caroline are initially drawn together as young analysts at the Wall Street firm Jane Street Capital by their mutual interest in effective altruism, the “earn to give” movement that gives “The Altruists” its name. (Characters affiliated with EA are frequently identified by their branded T-shirts.) The two encourage each other’s most dangerous instincts, like going all in on every bet because it’s “mathematically optimal” or refusing to communicate discomfort around Sam’s autocratic tendencies or Caroline’s polyamory. The plot frames Sam and Caroline’s slide into criminality as the slow corruption of self-identified “good guys,” though the show is strangely uncritical of the starting premise that the best way to make positive change in the world is by amassing a personal fortune.

	For all EA comes into focus, cryptocurrency itself remains stubbornly obscure. It’s not easy to mine drama from complex financial instruments, but “The Altruists” puts frustratingly little effort into explaining the water these crazy kids are swimming in. Without a more defined sense of what makes crypto unique, “The Altruists” is left with a faint rehash of the techno-optimism-gone-awry narrative already explored in series like “The Dropout,” “Super Pumped” and “WeCrashed,” which tellingly dropped within weeks of each other in 2022 (and just a few months before FTX flamed out). Those three titles collectively worked to capture a specific time and place; with its personal focus, “The Altruists” never does the same.

	“The Altruists” even gestures at more productive angles on the whole FTX affair than the folie a deux of Sam and Caroline. Potential framing devices, like a Bloomberg reporter’s investigation, are flirted with and abandoned. Nishad Singh (Karan Soni), SBF’s childhood friend turned employee, tells us that Sam’s Stanford Law professor parents Joe (Paul Reiser) and Barbara (Robin Weigert) are the skeleton key to his need to prove himself. “They already love you,” Nishad says of the scholars. “They just don’t fucking like you.” It’s a great line, just not one backed up in any way by the show’s portrayal of that relationship, which is fairly minimal and fails to lay the groundwork for head-scratching decisions like Joe and Barbara’s total credulity toward their son, both before and after his arrest.
	

	It’s not like “The Altruists” lacks time to explore the Bankman-Fried household dynamics. (The resources to convincingly render far-flung locations like Macau and Malta do, however, seem scarce.) At eight hourlong episodes, “The Altruists” is padded out with detours into Nishad’s office romance and the backstory of SBF’s college pal Sam Trabucco (Alex Lawther), who left FTX before things hit the fan. The space would be far better spent building out the crypto universe, shading in Sam and Caroline outside one another’s orbit or even outlandish incidents like FTX’s Larry David-starring Super Bowl ad. Without a stronger center, though, these satellite plots feel like they’re orbiting a vacuum.

	All eight episodes of “The Altruists” are now streaming on Netflix.

schema.headline: ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix FTX Series Fails to Get a Handle on Crypto Scammer Sam Bankman-Fried

title: ‘Boys by the River,’ an IDFA Highlight, Captures One Day in ‘Paradise’ in Europe, Relished by Three Afghan Asylum Seekers
description: Many films about migrants depict their travails. Richly textured and carefully structured, observational doc-fiction “Boys by the River” (“Ragazzi
body:
Many films about migrants depict their travails. Richly textured and carefully structured, observational doc-fiction “Boys by the River” (“Ragazzi al fiume”), which world premieres in IDFA’s Envision Competition directed by Switzerland-based Pablo Briones, captures one day spent by three Afghan asylum seekers in Switzerland by a river which one calls “paradise.”

	That said, the film also takes in the pressures of their currents lives and in interview voiceover, a sense of their tragic and even dramatic pasts. That is done, however, with a later discretion and sense of intimacy than found in many documentaries. This past is, moreover, gradually replaced by an uplifting sentiment, coursing the film, of the boys’ present dream: To live in peace.
	

	In a larger picture, “Boys by the River” captures one way so many international documentaries are going: Melding facets of fiction and documentary observation to forge themes and emotions.

	“Boys by the River” transpires over one hot Summer’s day near the Federal Asylum Centre in Balerna/Novazzano, the southernmost part of Ticino and Switzerland.

	Ahmad visits Farhad in his flat, telling him Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Migration has decreed that, given Afghanistan is considered safe enough for return, under certain circumstances young male Afghans could be deported back there from mid-April 2026. Ahmad is highly concerned, Farhad more nonplussed.

	The two friends walk through an industrial state and then a long pedestrian tunnel to emerge in fields and then stunning Alpine forest, with cliffs, streams, a river and a mesmeric waterfall. Joined by a third young Afghan, Hameed, they spend the whole day there, swimming, dozing, meeting a couple and their children, talking in desultory fashion.
	

	Most of “Boys by the River” is exactly that: Ahmad, Farhad and Hameed lazing, having fun at a extraordinary forest river.As they do, however, an fragmentary voiceover hears them talking about the horrors of their past.

	At one moment, Hameed, now caught sleeping in the sun, describes how he and some other 500 refugees, as they attempt to cross the border from Iran to Turkey, were shot at by the Turkish place who used real bullets.

	To bring larger sense and sentiment to the film, Briones captures images with a larger resonance, such as Ahmad and Farhad walk through the dark tunnel, the green forest ahead of them, which becomes a metaphor for Ahmad’s odyssey from Afghanistan, both geographic and psychological, recalls by a few words from hm on VoiceOver during a getting on for two minutes single shot: “Border, desert,.mountains, forest, police. camps, boat, water, fear , fear of cops, fear of animals, fear of getting lost, fear of dying.”

	Produced by two bastions of Swiss film production, Geneva’s Intermezzo Films (“Dreamers,” “Sonita,” “Before Summer Ends”) and Ticino’s “Cinédokké (“The Chilean,”)

	Sonita won the 2015 IDFA Audience Award and Sundance 2016 World Cinema – Documentary Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award. “Before Summer Ends” played Cannes ACID section a year later.

	Recent Cinédokké films include Locarno Piazza Grande title “Semret” and Sergio Castro-San Martín’s “The Chilean,” one of the most prominent titles in this year’s Locarno main competition.

	Briones fielded questions from Variety as he presented “Boys by the River” at Amsterdam’s IDFA.



	

					‘Boys by the River’ 
	



	“Boys by the River” takes some important directorial decisions such as Ahmad, Farhad and Hameed recalling the horrors of their past in brief conversation or voiceover commentary. Why this structural decision?

	I wanted the film to unfold as a day by the river, where we first meet them as young men enjoying that place. But knowing someone also means learning something of what they carry. Some memories were shared at my home, without a camera, once we had built trust. I chose to bring them into the film sparingly, so their past could resonate with the present without defining them through suffering or reproducing the interrogations asylum seekers endure.
	

	Though shot in observational style, the film has multiple poetic details which, for spectators looking for them, could have larger resonance, from a forest robot to a lone apple bobbing down a stream, swept by forces beyond control – rather the state of the Afghan boys. Could you comment?

	Observation, for me, happens before filming as much as during it. The poetic elements grow from that attention to reality. One day, while swimming there with my children, an apple floated past us. It immediately found its way into the script. Water flows without borders; the apple makes that movement visible, without locking it into one meaning. The robot belongs to another thread of the boys’ reality: surveillance and control that follow them wherever they go.

	Again, in terms of direction, you often shot the Afghan refugees in mid long-shot, against the background of the tunnel or forest, for example. Again, could you comment?

	I think we experience life largely through a wide view: we see people within a landscape, notice how they move, then sometimes draw closer. I wanted the film to share that way of looking. The river, the forest and the tunnel inspired me even before I met the boys. Filming them at a distance also gives them space, and allows the moments when we come very close to their faces or skin to become more intimate.

	How would you place “Boys by the River” in your career and the kinds of films you are interested in making?

	With “Boys by the River,” I could explore my love of fixed frames, carefully composed images, and the passage of time within a scene. I also ventured a little further into fiction, not to simulate reality, but to get closer to it or question it, sometimes even playfully. That space between documentary and fiction is where I want to keep working, though funding categories often try to force us to define and limit a film long before we can make it.

title: Ex-ESPN Personality Bonnie-Jill Laflin's Animal Rescue Suspended Over Missing Animal Records
description:
Ex-ESPN's Bonnie-Jill Laflin
                          Rescue Suspended, Accused of Failing to Tr
body:
Ex-ESPN's Bonnie-Jill Laflin
                          Rescue Suspended, Accused of Failing to Track 23 Animals
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            7:05 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              ESPN personality Bonnie-Jill Laflin's animal rescue organization has been suspended from pulling animals out of Los Angeles County shelters ... after officials say it failed to properly account for more than 20 ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
              The L.A. County Department of Animal Care and Control tells TMZ ... it suspended Hounds & Heroes Rescue's pull privileges in April 2026 after finding the organization failed to submit complete monthly placement reports for 23 animals pulled between February and April.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Officials say the reports are required to identify where the animals are -- whether they're being fostered or have been adopted.
      

              DACC also says it received allegations that some animals pulled by the rescue were subsequently left at other facilities, and claims multiple attempts to contact Laflin about the missing records went unanswered.
      
    
              The move comes amid a separate legal battle we told you about ... in which a dog boarding facility filed a lawsuit against Laflin and Hounds & Heroes, claiming the rescue left 14 dogs at its facility and failed to pay roughly $70,000 in boarding and care costs.
      
    
              The lawsuit also alleged one dog died while at the facility.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Hounds & Heroes fired back at the lawsuit, telling TMZ the org. "is aware of the complaint and firmly disputes its allegations. The Foundation will respond through the appropriate legal channels and will not comment further on pending litigation."
      
    
              They reiterate, in response to DACC's report ... "Our commitment remains unwavering: rescuing animals, protecting their welfare, and serving the veterans who depend on them."

title: Taylor Swift Returns to CMA Awards Stage After 13-Year Absence
description:
Taylor Swift
                          Takes CMA Stage with Throwback Mashup!!!
body:
Taylor Swift
                          Takes CMA Stage with Throwback Mashup!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            6:42 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
              Taylor Swift is back where her country music career took off ... delivering a nostalgic performance at the CMA Awards with a mashup of two fan favorites, "Our Song" and "I Knew It, I Knew You."
      
    
      
      Taylor Swift performs a mashup of “Our Song” and “I Knew It, I Knew You” at the #CMAAwards.
(via ABC/CMAs) https://t.co/wfuYZ52xa6
              @Variety
          
  
    
              Taylor returned to the CMA stage Wednesday night in Nashville for the first time in 13 years ... and considering 13 is her lucky number, the timing couldn't have been more fitting, especially as she mashed up one of her earliest country hits with her latest release.
      
    
              The showgirl popped out performing in an orange skirt and cowboy boots while strumming a blue guitar decorated with Toy Story clouds.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The appearance also comes at an interesting time for Taylor ... she's campaigning for Oscar glory with "I Knew It, I Knew You," which was written for "Toy Story 5."
      
    
              However, the night came with a bit of a letdown for Taylor ... as she lost out on Single of the Year to rising star Ella Langley, whose hit "Choosin' Texas" beat out Taylor's track for the coveted honor.
      
    
              Still, Taylor's got plenty more awards opportunities ahead ... she's scored five nominations at the 2027 Grammys, including Best Song Written for Visual Media.
      
    
              One thing's for sure, this pop star proved she's got plenty of love for her country roots ... reminding everyone before she conquered pop music and Hollywood, she was Nashville's golden girl.

title: Hila Klein Says She Can't Look at Estranged Husband Ethan in New Video Statement
description:
Hila Klein
                          I Can't Even Look at Ethan ...
                          How
body:
Hila Klein
                          I Can't Even Look at Ethan ...
                          How Are We Going to Co-Parent???
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            6:53 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              Hila Klein is finally ready to dive into the details of her split from Ethan Klein after his alleged affair ... and she says she can't even look at the guy.
      
    
              The popular internet personality shared a 30-minute video diving into the nitty-gritty of her pending divorce ... and she reiterated her claims that Ethan had a six-month affair with another woman.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Hila quickly became emotional in the clip ... saying she's not sure how she's going to get through this period and move on from the trauma of being betrayed by someone so close to her -- especially when she always imagined growing old at his side.
      

              She then said she doesn't know how she and Ethan are going to co-parent their 3 kids ... because she "can't look at him or talk to him."
      
    
              Hila admitted her life is full of uncertainty. She doesn't know where she'll live or what she'll do for work ... and she's also worried about what will happen to the people she employs.
      
    
              She also claimed she didn't want to speak out about her divorce ... but alleged that other people's narratives forced her to tell her side of the story.
      
    
              As we reported ... Hila publicly accused Ethan of having an affair last month in an Instagram statement -- to which Ethan asked people to respect his family's privacy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              He also said, "[My family has] nothing to do with this and share in your outrage and disappointment. Thank you," which many saw as a tacit acknowledgement of Hila's allegations, and he promised to remove any and all stake in the couple's "H3 Podcast."
      
    
              Hila filed for divorce shortly after their statements on social media ... and Ethan has since asked a judge not to award her spousal support.
      
    
              Basically, this doesn't sound like an amicable split ... so don't be surprised if these two end up sniping at each other regularly.

title: Dolly Parton’s Niece Honors Late Singer at CMAs with Custom Dress
description:
Dolly Parton
                          Niece Honors Late Singer in Custom Dress at CMAs
body:
Dolly Parton
                          Niece Honors Late Singer in Custom Dress at CMAs
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            5:25 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 18, 2026
                                7:31 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Dolly Parton’s niece brought a personal piece of the country legend to the CMA Awards ... stepping onto the red carpet in an outfit originally created for her late aunt.
      
    
              Danielle Parton attended Wednesday’s ceremony in Nashville wearing a white, long-sleeved dress with gold embellishments and sparkling fringe ... finishing the look with metallic gold boots. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              And the story behind the sparkle made the outfit even more special ... Danielle told Taste of Country ahead of the show the dress was made for Dolly for “Light of a Clear Blue Morning,” which recently earned a Grammy nomination.
      
    
              According to Danielle, Dolly had tried it on, but never got to wear it for its intended occasion. Her niece decided the CMAs would be the perfect opportunity to give it a meaningful debut. 
      
    
              Speaking to On the Red Carpet, Danielle credited Dolly’s longtime costume designer Steve Summers with creating the outfit ... joking, “they poured me into it tonight,” before explaining she wanted to honor her aunt by wearing it. 
      
    
              The tribute comes after Dolly died in August at 80. Danielle was named brand ambassador for her aunt’s estate last month ... taking on a public role in helping preserve her legacy.
      
    
              A little family history ... and a whole lot of Dolly sparkle.

title: Bill Cosby's Alleged Victim Asks Judge to Stop Him From Selling His Home
description:
Bill Cosby's Alleged Victim
                          Don't Let Him Sell His House, Judge!!!
body:
Bill Cosby's Alleged Victim
                          Don't Let Him Sell His House, Judge!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            4:15 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Joan Tarshis -- a woman who has accused Bill Cosby of sexual assault -- is asking a judge to stop him from selling or transferring any real estate ... claiming in a new legal filing that he's shown he won’t use it to pay verdicts against him.
      
    
              Tarshis' lawyer filed the document on Tuesday ... claiming that, based on news reports, the disgraced comedian has knocked about $2 million off the listing price of one of his New York City homes, dropping the ask from roughly $7 million to around $5 million.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              In addition, the lawyer cites a report that Cosby has failed to pay any of the $59.25 million judgment awarded to Donna Motsinger in California ... arguing that any claim that Cosby's selling the home to fulfill that debt isn't supported by past actions.
      

              We reported on Tarshis' original lawsuit back in 2023 ... in which she alleges he drugged and sexually assaulted her on two occasions in the early 1970s.
      
    
              She says she was disoriented on one occasion ... waking up amid Cosby allegedly trying to take her clothes off. She says she tried to fight him off ... before he allegedly overpowered her and forced his penis in her mouth.
      
    
              On another occasion, she says she went out with him to a music festival ... when she was given a drink that she claims made her lose consciousness. Tarshis claims she later woke up naked in bed next to Cosby ... and that she felt she’d been penetrated vaginally and anally.
